segments.text: Amazon S3 can be used to store all sorts
of data, including critical logs,
backups, and even compliance data. So
for workloads that require this type of
information that should never be changed
or deleted, at least for a period of
time, we can use a feature called S3
object lock. Object lock lets you store
objects using a worm model, which is
short for write once, read many. So
after an object is locked, no one is
able to overwrite or delete it until
that lock expires, not even the root
user or administrators. That makes this
a very powerful security feature. So
let's talk about it and how it works. To
start using object lock, we can navigate
to the S3 dashboard, click on an
existing bucket or create a new one, and
then head to properties and then scroll
down until we see object lock. So by
default it will always be disabled but
we can edit to enable it. So keep in
mind that this feature only works on
version buckets. So you would have to
enable versioning first and then once we
enable object lock we can then select
the default retention to either be
disabled or enabled. And if we select
enable we can then set the default
retention mode to either be governance
or compliance.
Compliance mode is the strictest option.
It offers the strongest protection. No
one can shorten or remove the retention
period. Not even admins or root users.
And no one can delete or overwrite the
object. Again, not even admins or root
users. That's how powerful it is. So,
this mode is typically used for
regulatory requirements or even for
immutable backups. Instead, governance
mode is a little bit more relaxed. It
prevents modification or deletion of an
object unless you have the proper
permissions to overwrite that. So
authorized users can override the
retention period if they have the proper
permissions. So this is a helpful mode
to protect objects from accidental
deletion or even from something like
ransomware. And it can also be used to
test your retention periods before
turning on the more stricter compliance
mode. So when should you choose which?
Well, if the exam question mentions
strict retention with tamperproofing or
that not even the root user can delete
that information, then the answer is
very clear. It's going to be compliance
mode. But if the scenario presented
mentions being able to override
settings, then it's probably looking for
governance mode. It just really depends
on the phrasing and some of the keywords
in the question and answers. But
regardless of which mode you select, we
can set a default retention period in
either days or years. So for example, we
could lock an object for 30 days, 1
year, 2 years, etc. With object lock,
there's also the ability to place a
legal hold on an object version. This is
going to be similar to a retention
period since a legal hold actually
prevents an object version from being
modified or deleted. But the difference
here is that a legal hold doesn't have a
fixed amount of time. So instead, it
remains in effect until you remove that
legal hold, which can be done with any
user or role that has the proper
permissions. You can have both a legal
hold and retention period on the same
object version at the same time because
they operate independently. So legal
holds are commonly used for things like
investigations, if you have any sort of
legal litigation, or even for external
audits of your data whenever you may not
know how long your object will need to
remain immutable. So back in the
console, we would finish enabling this
feature and then whenever we upload
objects, the configured settings would
apply. to enable legal hold on objects.
You would then use the S3 put object
legal hold permission and API call. So
let's wrap up by talking about use cases
and scenarios that you might find on the
exam and on the job. The first one is
going to be protecting cloud trail logs
from deletion and tampering. Here we can
do a few things. We can store logs in a
dedicated bucket and account as we've
already learned. We can then enable
object lock in compliance mode and then
we can apply a retention period say for
example 6 months 1 year etc. And this
would prevent attackers from being able
to cover their tracks even if they gain
access to that centralized account and
it would help prevent accidental
deletions.
As another use case and scenario let's
say that we want immutable backups for
ransomware protection. You would apply
the same steps as in the prior scenario
and then you would use governance or
compliance modes depending on the
strictness level that you want. And by
doing this, backups would not be able to
be overwritten or deleted during that
retention period, even if the attacker
takes over your account, unless it's in
governance mode and they have those
permissions, of course. Finally, for our
last use case, let's say that we have
forensics and legal investigations that
are going on here. We can use legal
holds to prevent deletion until the
investigation is complete which we don't
necessarily know when that will be. So
with legal holds we have that
flexibility.
So to recap as we wrap up remember that
you can enable object lock on version
buckets. You can choose governance mode
for flexible retention or you can choose
compliance mode for strict enforcement.
You can set retention periods and you
can also set legal holds whenever
needed. And this feature is going to be
great for things like logs like your
cloud trail logs or cloudatch logs for
backups for forensics data or any other
type of critical or sensitive
information. But with that, let's go
